c.tagline: A belle-époque spa town on the edge of the Black Forest, where thermal baths and a grand casino have drawn European royalty for two centuries

card: Contactless and card payment are the norm at hotels, restaurants, and the casino; small cafes, market stalls, and some spa facilities may prefer cash, so carry a little euros.

taxi.fareNote: Metered fares are standard; airport transfers to Karlsruhe/Baden-Baden Airport or Stuttgart are usually flat-rate — confirm before boarding

emergency.note: 112 is the EU-wide emergency number and reaches English-speaking dispatchers in most cases

english.label: Easy to get by in English

walk: The compact spa-town core between the Kurhaus, casino, and Lichtentaler Allee is entirely walkable and pedestrian-friendly; the Old Town's hillside lanes involve some gentle climbing, and Merkur mountain is reached by a short funicular rather than on foot.

safety.safety: Very safe; Baden-Baden is a genteel resort town with very low crime and is comfortable for solo travelers at any hour
safety.crime: Petty theft is rare; the main caution is standard care with valuables in busy tourist areas like the casino and spa lockers

hood_landmark.Altstadt (Old Town): Stiftskirche and the New Castle hillside
hood_landmark.Lichtental: Lichtentaler Allee promenade and Kloster Lichtenthal abbey
hood_landmark.Weststadt / Rebland: Vineyard slopes toward the Rhine valley

hood_desc: The elegant heart of the spa town, centered on the Kurhaus, casino, and grand 19th-century hotels — the natural base for most visitors and home to the thermal baths.
The hillside medieval core above the spa quarter, with narrow lanes, the Stiftskirche, and the New Castle offering panoramic views over the town.
A quiet, leafy district along the Lichtentaler Allee promenade, anchored by the historic Cistercian abbey and rose gardens — a peaceful, residential contrast to the casino district.
The wine-growing fringe toward the Rhine valley, dotted with vineyards and a more local, less touristy pace.
A hilltop village a short drive or hike above town, known for its ruined castle and sweeping Black Forest views.

water.note: Tap water is excellent and safe to drink.

transit.pay: Contactless card, KVV app, or cash on board; day tickets available
transit.map: Route maps at kvv.de and posted at bus stops
transit.note: The compact center is easily walkable; buses mainly serve outlying districts like Ebersteinburg and Rebland

transport.air: Baden-Baden Karlsruhe Airport (FKB), ~10 km away, with flights on Ryanair and others to European cities; Stuttgart Airport (STR) is a larger alternative about 1 hour away
transport.train: Baden-Baden station has ICE high-speed connections to Frankfurt (~1.5 hrs), Basel, and Karlsruhe; the station is about 15 minutes from the town center by bus or taxi
transport.bus: FlixBus and regional coaches connect Baden-Baden to Stuttgart, Karlsruhe, and Strasbourg
transport.ferry: None — Baden-Baden is inland with no ferry service
transport.car: Easily reached via the A5 autobahn; parking in the compact center is limited, so many hotels offer valet or garage parking

airport.name: Baden-Baden Karlsruhe Airport
airport.transport: Airport shuttle bus timed to flights; taxi transfer roughly €25-35

net.m: Excellent 4G/5G coverage throughout Baden-Baden and the surrounding Black Forest foothills
net.w: Free wifi standard in hotels, cafes, and the Kurhaus
net.fwn: Free wifi widely available in cafes and public spaces in the town center
net.ap: EU roaming covers most European visitors; a prepaid German SIM or eSIM is easy to buy at the airport or a phone shop for others

tip.s: Not obligatory; rounding up or a small tip for spa attendants and hotel staff is appreciated
tip.r: 5-10% is customary if service isn't already included — hand the tip directly to the server rather than leaving it on the table

food.name: Schwarzwaelder Kirschtorte (Black Forest gateau)
food.desc: Layers of chocolate sponge soaked in Kirschwasser with sour cherries and cream. The real regional version is boozy, not sweet.

places.name: Klosterschaenke Lichtenthal

places.name: Weinstube im Baldreit
places.note: Runs a proper Spargelkarte in season, matched to Baden white wines.

places.name: Klosterschaenke Lichtenthal

places.note: Spargel served in the beer garden all season, generous and unfussy.

places.name: Gasthaus zum Rebstock

places.name: Rizzi Wine Bistro and Restaurant

landmarks: Kurhaus and Casino Baden-Baden
Marlene Dietrich called it the world's most beautiful casino; its gilded, chandelier-hung salons anchor the spa town's neoclassical Kurhaus.
Friedrichsbad
A palatial 1877 Roman-Irish bathhouse where bathers progress through 17 marble-and-fresco stages of steam, soaks, and showers.
Caracalla Spa (Caracalla Therme)
A modern thermal complex fed by the town's ancient hot springs, with indoor-outdoor pools, grottoes, and saunas beneath the Black Forest hills.
Lichtentaler Allee
A ravishing 2.3-kilometer riverside promenade of exotic trees, rose gardens, and villas, strolled by European aristocracy for two centuries.
Trinkhalle (Pump Room)
A colonnaded 19th-century pump house whose 90-meter arcade is lined with romantic frescoes of Black Forest legends.
Merkur Mountain
Baden-Baden's local peak, reached by one of Germany's steepest funiculars, with paragliders, trails, and views across the Rhine plain.
Hohenbaden Castle (Altes Schloss)
The evocative clifftop ruin of the margraves' medieval seat, free to explore, with a wind harp and stunning valley panoramas.
Museum Frieder Burda
Richard Meier's luminous white gallery on Lichtentaler Allee, showing blue-chip modern art from Picasso to Gerhard Richter.
Stiftskirche (Collegiate Church)
The pink-towered parish church on the old marketplace, sheltering the tombs of Baden's margraves above the town's Roman bath ruins.
Lichtenthal Abbey (Kloster Lichtenthal)
A serene Cistercian convent founded in 1245 at the end of the Allee, still home to nuns selling handmade liqueurs.

train.note: Trains use Baden-Baden station, which is not in the spa town at all but out in the Oos district a few kilometres north-west; city buses run from the station forecourt to Leopoldsplatz and the Kurhaus in about 15 minutes. Around 43 of the 140-odd daily trains are long-distance, so the service is far better than the town's size suggests. One TGV pair a day has linked Baden-Baden with Strasbourg, Lyon and Marseille since 2012, and the two-hourly ICE 12 runs south through Freiburg to Basel, Zurich, Bern and Interlaken. French TGV seats on the Frankfurt-Marseille run are sold as a fixed-price reservation-only fare and sell out, so book ahead rather than turning up.

bus.note: Long-distance coaches stop at the bus station beside Baden-Baden railway station in Oos, so you have the same transfer into town as rail passengers. FlixBus is effectively the only operator and tickets are bought online; there is no staffed counter. Karlsruhe is about 30 minutes away by coach and Strasbourg roughly 1h15, and for anything further afield it is usually quicker to connect through Karlsruhe or Frankfurt.

ferry.note: Baden-Baden is an inland spa town in the Black Forest foothills with only the small Oosbach running through it, so there are no ferries or passenger boats. The nearest scheduled water transport is on the Rhine, about 20 km west, where local river crossings and Strasbourg sightseeing boats operate.

half.name: Strasbourg
half.blurb: A French city on the German border with a Gothic sandstone cathedral and a canal-laced old town of half-timbered Alsatian houses.

half.name: Heidelberg
half.blurb: A university town on the Neckar River overlooked by a ruined Renaissance castle and known for its long cobbled old town.

half.name: Freiburg im Breisgau
half.blurb: A university city on the edge of the Black Forest with a Gothic minster and small open canals called Bächle running through its streets.

half.name: Karlsruhe
half.blurb: A city laid out in a fan pattern radiating from a Baroque palace, with a moated castle and formal gardens at its center.

half.name: Triberg
half.blurb: A Black Forest town famous for Germany's highest waterfall and for its role in the history of the cuckoo clock.
